extracted.intended_audience: students learning introductory logic (undergraduate or advanced-high-school level)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for understanding, translating, and reasoning with conditional and biconditional connectives and with quantifiers (∀, ∃). Covers truth tables, equivalences, translating English to symbolic form, scope and binding of variables, and methods for testing validity/equivalence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-table for conditional (P → Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditional P → Q should be true in every case except when P is true and Q is false; that is, P → Q is false only on the line where P true and Q false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fill undetermined lines so that for any instance (e.g., P(x) → Q(x) for all x) the conditional comes out true unless you can find a case with P true and Q false. Examples: 'If x > 2 then x^2 > 4' leads to making lines with P false (regardless of Q) true. Use truth-table rows to check whether desired informal claims (like 'always true') match this table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence P → Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula P → Q is equivalent to ¬P ∨ Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive equivalence via truth tables and use it to rewrite conditionals as disjunctions when convenient. Examples and heuristics: teacher's threat 'You won't neglect your homework, or you'll fail' is grammatically ¬P ∨ Q and can express P → Q in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence P → Q ≡ ¬(P ∧ ¬Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: The formula P → Q is equivalent to ¬(P ∧ ¬Q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use double negation and De Morgan's laws to transform ¬P ∨ Q into ¬(P ∧ ¬Q). Interpretively, saying P → Q is asserting that there is no case in which P is true and Q false (e.g., no x with P(x) ∧ ¬Q(x)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modus ponens validity (P → Q, P ⊢ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument form with premises P → Q and P and conclusion Q should be valid (modus ponens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use truth-table analysis: premises are both true only in the line where conclusion is also true. This supports the chosen truth-table for the conditional. Changing the conditional truth-table (e.g., making different rows false) would make intuitively valid arguments invalid or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirming the consequent is invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: From premises P → Q and Q it is not valid to infer P (affirming the consequent is a fallacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth-table shows a line where both premises true and conclusion false. Use concrete counterexamples (e.g., Jones goes to jail for reasons other than murder) to illustrate invalidity. This distinguishes P → Q from Q → P (converse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Converse vs contrapositive distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The converse Q → P is not equivalent to P → Q, while the contrapositive ¬Q → ¬P is equivalent to P → Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check equivalence with truth tables; use examples to show the difference (converse may be false even when original conditional is true). Use contrapositive law often in mathematical proofs since ¬Q → ¬P conveys the same information as P → Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional definition (P ↔ Q)
rubrics_metrics.description: P ↔ Q abbreviates (P → Q) ∧ (Q → P); it expresses 'P if and only if Q' (iff), i.e., P is necessary and sufficient for Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify biconditional truth table as conjunction of the two conditionals. Also useful equivalence: P ↔ Q ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (¬P ∧ ¬Q). In mathematics, use 'iff' or 'necessary and sufficient' explicitly whenever a biconditional is intended; do not assume an if-then is an iff in mathematical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common English phrasings mapped to P → Q
rubrics_metrics.description: Several English expressions correspond to P → Q: 'P implies Q', 'Q, if P', 'P only if Q', 'P is a sufficient condition for Q', 'Q is a necessary condition for P'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand each mapping: e.g., 'P only if Q' means ¬Q → ¬P which by contrapositive is equivalent to P → Q. Use these translations when converting English prose into symbolic logic and beware of subtle differences in ordinary language vs. mathematical precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate English conditionals carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating natural-language conditional statements into symbols, identify the intended antecedent and consequent, and consider conversational implicatures (people often mean iff when they say if).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work by introducing propositional abbreviations and rewriting stepwise. Examples: 'Either John went to the store, or we're out of eggs' (P ∨ Q) often is intended as ¬P → Q in conversational inference. In mathematics, insist on explicit iff when biconditional is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meanings of quantifiers ∀ and ∃
rubrics_metrics.description: ∀x P(x) means P(x) is true for every x in the universe (universal quantifier). ∃x P(x) means there exists at least one x in the universe for which P(x) is true (existential quantifier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret quantifiers in terms of truth sets: ∀x P(x) ↔ truth set of P equals universe; ∃x P(x) ↔ truth set nonempty. Use examples (∀x (x^2 ≥ 0) true in R; ∃x (x^2−2x+3=0) false in R) to test understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound vs free variables; binding by quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantifiers bind variables: a variable bound by a quantifier is not free and can be renamed without changing meaning; variables not bound by a quantifier are free and affect truth relative to assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in ∀x L(x,y), x is bound and y is free — the formula asserts 'everyone likes y' (a statement about y). Use fresh variable names to avoid confusion when nesting quantifiers (e.g., replace ∃y M(x,y) by ∃z M(x,z)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope convention for quantifiers and logical connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The expressions ∀x and ∃x apply only to the statement that immediately follows. For instance, ∀x P(x) → Q(x) is to be read as (∀x P(x)) → Q(x), not ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit with parentheses when needed. When translating natural language, decide whether the quantifier governs the whole conditional or just the antecedent/consequent and mark scope accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating English quantifier statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use existential quantifier for words like 'someone', 'there exists', and universal quantifier for 'everyone', 'everything'. Translate compound claims by combining quantifiers with logical connectives and relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceed stepwise: identify the outer logical structure, then translate subphrases. Examples: 'Everything in that store is overpriced or poorly made' → ∀x [S(x) → (O(x) ∨ P(x))]. Use predicate letters and specified constants for named individuals (e.g., j for Joe, s for Susan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiple quantifiers and order sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Order of quantifiers matters: ∀x∃y φ(x,y) can have a different truth value than ∃y∀x φ(x,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze nested quantifiers one at a time, from left to right: treat the outer quantifier as ranging over statements that contain the inner quantifier. Use concrete examples (e.g., ∀x∃y (x+y=5) true in R; ∃y∀x (x+y=5) false) to see the distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressing set-relations with quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Set relations can be written with quantifiers: A ⊆ B as ∀x (x ∈ A → x ∈ B); disjointness of A and C  ackslash B as ¬∃x (x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ C ∧ x ∉ B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use definitions of intersection, difference, subset, etc., and translate them into predicate form using appropriate quantifiers and connectives. Examples and exercise problems demonstrate this process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity in natural-language quantifier words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'anyone', 'anyone who', or 'anyone in the dorm' can be ambiguous (sometimes meaning 'someone', sometimes 'everyone'); interpret in context and rephrase to decide between ∃ and ∀.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When in doubt, rewrite the English sentence explicitly using 'someone' or 'everyone', then translate. Examples: 'Anyone who has a friend who has the measles will be quarantined' is a universal claim (∀x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using truth tables to test validity and equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct truth tables to check whether argument forms are valid or whether formulas are logically equivalent (e.g., P → Q vs ¬P ∨ Q, or to check that a proposed truth-table choice yields intuitive validities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply truth-table analysis to simple argument forms (e.g., see Figures 4 and 5) and for equivalence checks (e.g., show P ↔ Q ≡ (P ∧ Q) ∨ (¬P ∧ ¬Q)). Use counterexamples derived from truth-tables to show invalidity (affirming the consequent) and to justify chosen truth-table rows.
